title: Reinforcement Learning with Python
subtitle: From the basics to Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly course on reinforcement learning: the core ideas, tabular Q-learning, DQN and PPO, then practical work with Gymnasium environments and Stable-Baselines3. Written for the current Gymnasium (1.x) API and recent Stable-Baselines3 2.x releases; check the library docs for your installed versions.

chapters.title: What is reinforcement learning?
summary: Reinforcement learning, or RL, is learning by trial and error. An agent takes actions in an environment, gets a reward signal, and slowly learns which actions lead to more reward over time.

Nobody gives the agent the right answers. Unlike supervised learning there are no labels, only a score that arrives after the fact, often delayed. The agent must work out which of its earlier actions deserve the credit or the blame.
In this course you learn the ideas first, then practice them in Python with Gymnasium, which provides environments, and Stable-Baselines3, which provides ready-made algorithms.

glossary.def: The learner and decision maker. In code it is usually a policy plus a learning algorithm.
Everything the agent interacts with. It reacts to actions and produces observations and rewards.
What the agent actually sees at a step. Often called the state when it contains everything that matters.
A choice the agent makes, such as push left or push right.
A single number the environment sends after each step. It says how good that step was.
The agent's rule for choosing actions from observations. Learning means improving the policy.
The total reward collected over time. The agent tries to maximize it, not just the next reward.
One run from a start state until the task ends, for example one game.

keyPoints: RL learns from rewards, not from labeled examples.
The loop is: observe, act, receive reward and next observation, repeat.
The goal is a high total return over time, not a high immediate reward.
Rewards can be delayed, so credit assignment is the hard part.
The agent must explore to find good actions, and exploit what it already knows.

items: ELI5. Reinforcement learning is learning by trying. An agent acts, sees what happens and a reward tells it how it did. Like training a dog: treats for good, nothing for bad, and over time it learns.

Imagine teaching a dog a trick. You cannot explain it in words. You wait for a good attempt and give a treat. Over many tries the dog connects what it did with the treat. That is reinforcement learning in one picture: the dog is the agent, the room is the environment, the treat is the reward.

Compare this with supervised learning. There, every example comes with the correct answer, like a photo labeled cat. In RL nobody tells the agent the correct move. It only learns afterwards whether things went well, and the result of an action can show up many steps later. A chess move may only prove good or bad twenty moves on.

lesson.code:
# The whole RL idea as pseudo-Python
observation = env.reset()
done = False
total = 0
while not done:
    action = policy(observation)          # the agent decides
    observation, reward, done = env.step(action)   # the world answers
    total += reward                       # keep score
# learning = changing policy so that total goes up next time

items: Where is RL used? Game playing, robot control, recommendation and ad systems, data center cooling, chip layout, and training language models from human feedback. It shines when you can simulate or safely try things many times, and when the right behavior is easier to score than to describe.
It is also hard. Rewards can be sparse, training can be unstable, and a clever agent will happily exploit a badly designed reward. Later chapters show how to spot and manage this.

Course plan. First the ideas: Gymnasium environments, the Markov decision process, exploration, and tabular Q-learning. Then deep RL with neural networks. Then Stable-Baselines3: PPO, DQN, SAC, evaluation, callbacks, logging and your own environments.

chapters.title: Python setup and Gymnasium basics

maps.title: Gymnasium at a glance
links: Environment | is trained on by | Stable-Baselines3 [ch8]

summary: Gymnasium is the maintained successor to OpenAI Gym. It gives every environment the same small interface, so any agent can be paired with any environment.

You create an environment with gym.make, start it with reset, and advance it with step. Step returns five values: observation, reward, terminated, truncated and info. Terminated means the task really ended; truncated means a time limit cut it off.

Every environment describes its inputs and outputs with spaces. Discrete spaces hold integers, Box spaces hold arrays of numbers. Knowing the spaces tells you which algorithms and network shapes you can use.

glossary.def: The Python library that defines the standard environment interface and ships many example environments.
Function that builds an environment from its name, for example CartPole-v1.
Starts a new episode and returns the first observation and an info dictionary.
Applies an action and returns observation, reward, terminated, truncated and info.
True when the episode ended because of the task itself, such as falling over or reaching the goal.
True when the episode was stopped by a limit such as a maximum number of steps, not by the task.
A space of n integers, 0 up to n minus 1. Used for a fixed set of choices.
A space of arrays of real numbers with lower and upper bounds. Used for continuous values.

keyPoints: Install with pip install gymnasium, and use a virtual environment.
reset returns (observation, info). step returns (observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info).
An episode is over when terminated or truncated is True.
Terminated and truncated are different: only truncation means the future was cut off, not that it was bad.
Pass a seed to reset to make runs repeatable.
env.action_space.sample() gives a random valid action, handy for testing.

items: ELI5. Gymnasium is a toy box of practice worlds with one shared way to talk to them: reset to start, step to act. Learn the two calls and you can try any world.
Start with a clean virtual environment, then install the library. Recent Stable-Baselines3 releases need Python 3.10 or newer, so use a current Python for the whole course.

lesson.code:
python -m venv rl-env
source rl-env/bin/activate        # Windows: rl-env\Scripts\activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install gymnasium
python -c "import gymnasium; print(gymnasium.__version__)"

items: Here is the first program. CartPole is a cart with a pole balanced on top. The agent pushes the cart left or right to keep the pole up. Each step the pole stays up gives a reward of 1.

lesson.code:
import gymnasium as gym

env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
obs, info = env.reset(seed=42)
print(env.observation_space)   # Box with 4 numbers
print(env.action_space)        # Discrete(2): 0 = push left, 1 = push right

total, done = 0.0, False
while not done:
    action = env.action_space.sample()            # random policy
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    total += reward
    done = terminated or truncated
print("episode return:", total)
env.close()

items: A random policy usually lasts only a few dozen steps. The four observation numbers are cart position, cart velocity, pole angle and pole angular velocity. The episode is terminated if the pole tilts past about twelve degrees or the cart leaves the track. In CartPole-v1 it is truncated at 500 steps, which is the best possible return.

Why two flags? If the pole falls, the future is worth nothing: that is termination. If time simply ran out, the situation was still fine and a learning algorithm should still value the future. Treating a time limit as a real end teaches wrong values, so Gymnasium keeps them separate.

lesson.code:
# Watching an episode needs a render mode
env = gym.make("CartPole-v1", render_mode="human")      # opens a window
env = gym.make("CartPole-v1", render_mode="rgb_array")  # returns images to save as video

# Other environments to try
gym.make("FrozenLake-v1")     # tiny grid, Discrete observations
gym.make("Taxi-v3")           # 500 discrete states
gym.make("Pendulum-v1")       # continuous action: Box
# LunarLander needs:  pip install "gymnasium[box2d]"

items: Spaces matter. Discrete(2) means two actions. Box(low, high, shape) means an array of real numbers, for example a torque between minus two and two. Value-based methods such as DQN need discrete actions. Algorithms such as SAC and TD3 are for continuous Box actions. PPO handles both.

chapters.title: Markov decision processes

maps.title: The MDP
links: Discount factor | turns rewards into | Return
Policy | is evaluated by | Value function
Value function [ch5] | is learned by | Q-learning [ch5]

summary: A Markov decision process, or MDP, is the math behind RL. It has states, actions, rules for how states change, rewards and a discount factor. The Markov property says the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the longer history.

The discount factor gamma, between zero and one, makes later rewards count less. The return is the sum of discounted rewards. A value function V(s) is the expected return from a state under a policy, and Q(s, a) is the expected return after taking action a in state s.
The Bellman equation says a value equals the immediate reward plus the discounted value of what follows. Almost every RL algorithm is a way of solving or approximating this equation.

glossary.def: Markov decision process: states, actions, transitions, rewards and a discount factor.
The future depends only on the current state and action, not on how you got there.
The rule, possibly random, for which state comes next after an action.
A number from 0 to 1 that shrinks future rewards. Close to 1 means far-sighted.
Sum of discounted rewards: r0 + gamma r1 + gamma squared r2 and so on.
Expected return starting in state s and following the policy.
Expected return from taking action a in state s, then following the policy.
Recursive relation: value equals reward plus discounted value of the next state.

keyPoints: An MDP is states, actions, transitions, rewards and gamma.
Return = r0 + gamma*r1 + gamma^2*r2 + ...
Gamma near 0 is short-sighted. Gamma near 1 is far-sighted. 0.99 is a common default.
V(s) scores states. Q(s, a) scores actions in states.
The best policy picks the action with the highest Q in every state.
If the observation hides important information, the problem is only partly observable and a plain MDP is not a perfect fit.

items: ELI5. A Markov decision process says: the world is in a state, you choose an action, you get a reward and a new state. What matters is only where you are now. It is the board on which all of RL is played.

Everything in the first chapter fits in one tidy model. At each time step the agent is in a state s, picks an action a, the world moves to a new state s prime with some probability, and a reward r arrives. Repeat.

The Markov property is a statement about the state, not about the world. If the state includes everything you need to predict what happens next, it is Markov. In CartPole, position and velocity of both cart and pole are enough. A single photo of the pole would not be, because it hides velocity. People then stack several frames.

Why discount? Two reasons. It keeps infinite sums finite, and it expresses a preference for sooner rewards. With gamma = 0.9, a reward of 10 that arrives three steps later is worth 10 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 = 7.29 now.

lesson.code:
def discounted_return(rewards, gamma):
    total = 0.0
    for t, r in enumerate(rewards):
        total += (gamma ** t) * r
    return total

print(discounted_return([1, 1, 1], 0.5))   # 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 1.75
print(discounted_return([0, 0, 8], 0.5))   # 8 * 0.25 = 2.0

items: Value functions answer: how good is it to be here? Q-values answer: how good is it to do this here? If you know Q for every state and action, acting is easy: pick the largest.

The Bellman idea: the return from now equals the reward now plus gamma times the return from the next state. So Q(s, a) = r + gamma x max over a prime of Q(s prime, a prime), when you act optimally afterwards. That one line is behind Q-learning in the next chapters, and DQN is the same idea with a neural network.

lesson.code:
# Bellman backup for one transition (optimal case)
#   Q(s, a)  <-  r + gamma * max_a' Q(s', a')
q_target = r + gamma * max(Q[s_next])

items: Finally, a policy can be deterministic (one action per state) or stochastic (a probability for each action). Stochastic policies help exploration and are used by PPO and A2C. Deterministic ones are often used at test time.

chapters.title: Exploration, exploitation and bandits

maps.title: Explore or exploit
links: Bandit | is an MDP with | One state

summary: An agent that always repeats the best action it knows may never discover a better one. An agent that always tries new things never cashes in. This is the exploration versus exploitation trade-off.

A multi-armed bandit is the simplest setting: one state, several actions, each paying a random reward. It isolates the trade-off. The agent keeps a running average of rewards per action and picks mostly the best one.
Epsilon-greedy is the classic rule: with probability epsilon pick a random action, otherwise pick the one with the highest estimate. Epsilon is often decayed over time. Deep RL uses the same idea.

glossary.def: Trying actions to learn more about them, even if they look worse right now.
Choosing the action that currently looks best to collect reward.
A problem with one state and several actions, each with an unknown reward distribution.
With probability epsilon act randomly, otherwise act greedily.
The action with the highest current value estimate.
Estimate of an action's value: the mean of the rewards seen so far for that action.
How much reward was lost compared to always picking the best action.

keyPoints: Without exploration the agent can lock onto a poor choice forever.
Estimate each action's value with a running average.
Incremental update: new_estimate = old + (reward - old) / count.
Epsilon-greedy is simple and works well. Typical epsilon is 0.1, or decays from 1.0 to a small value.
Random start estimates or optimistic start values also push exploration.
Evaluate a trained agent greedily, with exploration turned off.

items: ELI5. Exploration is trying new things; exploitation is using what works. Like choosing between your favourite restaurant and a new one. Bandits are the simplest version of this tension.

Picture five slot machines with different, hidden average payouts. You have 1000 pulls. Pull one machine only and you may never learn another was better. Pull all machines equally forever and you waste pulls on bad ones. The art is in between.
The agent keeps two lists: the estimated value of each arm and how many times it has pulled it. After a pull with reward r, it updates the average without storing history.

lesson.code:
import random

n_arms = 5
Q = [0.0] * n_arms        # value estimates
N = [0] * n_arms          # pull counts

def choose(epsilon):
    if random.random() < epsilon:
        return random.randrange(n_arms)             # explore
    return max(range(n_arms), key=lambda a: Q[a])   # exploit

def update(arm, reward):
    N[arm] += 1
    Q[arm] += (reward - Q[arm]) / N[arm]            # running average

items: Choosing epsilon. Too small and learning is slow to find better arms. Too large and you keep wasting pulls. A common schedule starts epsilon high and decays it linearly. Stable-Baselines3's DQN does exactly this with the parameters exploration_fraction and exploration_final_eps.

Bandits matter beyond slot machines: choosing which ad to show, which article to recommend, or which version of a web page to test. Full RL adds the idea that actions also change the future state, which is what the next chapters add.
Try the Bandit Lab in the practice section. Pull the arms by hand first, then switch on epsilon-greedy and watch the estimates settle.

chapters.title: Tabular Q-learning
summary: Q-learning learns the action values Q(s, a) from experience. Keep a table with one row per state and one column per action. After each step, move the table entry a little toward the target: reward plus gamma times the best value in the next state.
The learning rate alpha sets how big that move is. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns about the greedy policy while behaving with an exploring policy such as epsilon-greedy.
Tables only work when the number of states is small and discrete, like FrozenLake with 16 states or Taxi with 500. Bigger problems need function approximation, which is the next big idea.

glossary.def: An array of shape (number of states, number of actions) holding the current Q estimates.
A method that updates Q toward reward plus gamma times the maximum Q of the next state.
How far each update moves the estimate toward the target. Between 0 and 1.
The value r + gamma * max Q(s', a') that the old estimate is nudged toward.
Target minus current estimate. The size of the surprise.
Learning about one policy (greedy) while following another (exploring).
A Gymnasium grid world: reach the goal over ice without falling into holes. Slippery by default.

keyPoints: Update: Q[s,a] += alpha * (r + gamma * max(Q[s']) - Q[s,a]).
At a terminal state there is no next value: the target is just r.
Behave with epsilon-greedy, evaluate with greedy.
Alpha around 0.1 to 0.5 and gamma around 0.9 to 0.99 are typical for small tasks.
FrozenLake is slippery: the same action can move you somewhere else, so expect noisy learning.
Tables do not scale: add one state variable and the table grows multiplicatively.

items: ELI5. Q-learning keeps a table of how good each action is in each state, and updates the number with each experience. It is like a notebook of scores for every move, slowly corrected.
Q-learning is the Bellman idea turned into a learning rule. You do not need a model of the environment. You just act, watch what happens and adjust.

Each experience is a tuple (s, a, r, s prime, done). From it compute a target: if the episode ended, the target is r. Otherwise it is r plus gamma times the best Q in s prime. The old estimate then moves a fraction alpha toward the target.

lesson.code:
import numpy as np
import gymnasium as gym

env = gym.make("FrozenLake-v1", is_slippery=False)   # deterministic version to start
n_s, n_a = env.observation_space.n, env.action_space.n
Q = np.zeros((n_s, n_a))
alpha, gamma = 0.5, 0.95
eps, eps_min, eps_decay = 1.0, 0.05, 0.999
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

for episode in range(5000):
    s, _ = env.reset()
    done = False
    while not done:
        if rng.random() < eps:
            a = env.action_space.sample()
        else:
            a = int(np.argmax(Q[s]))
        s2, r, terminated, truncated, _ = env.step(a)
        target = r if terminated else r + gamma * np.max(Q[s2])
        Q[s, a] += alpha * (target - Q[s, a])
        s, done = s2, terminated or truncated
    eps = max(eps_min, eps * eps_decay)

policy = np.argmax(Q, axis=1)     # greedy policy: best action for each state

items: Notice the line that uses terminated, not truncated, to cut off the future. A time-limit truncation should still bootstrap from the next state, because the future was not actually zero.

FrozenLake action numbers are 0 left, 1 down, 2 right, 3 up. The default map is four by four with a start in the top left and a goal in the bottom right. With is_slippery=True the move only goes the intended way a third of the time, so learning needs many more episodes and the best success rate is well below 100 percent.

Why is it off-policy? The max in the target assumes you act greedily from the next state, even though you actually explored. That lets Q-learning learn the optimal values while still exploring. SARSA, a close relative, uses the action actually taken instead and is called on-policy.
Open the Gridworld Lab in the practice section. Train the agent for a few hundred episodes and watch the arrows turn toward the goal.

summary: To teach an agent your own task you write a Gymnasium environment: a class that subclasses gym.Env, declares its observation and action spaces, and implements reset and step.

Spaces must match the data you return exactly, including shape and dtype. Stable-Baselines3 provides check_env to catch mistakes early. Fix every warning before training, because bad environments waste hours.
Wrappers add behavior around an existing environment without editing it: limit time, scale rewards, clip actions, stack frames. They are small and composable.

A wrapper that truncates episodes after a maximum number of steps. Applied via max_episode_steps.
A dictionary for extra data. The agent should not learn from it, but you can log it.

Prefer wrappers over editing environment code when you only change data going in or out.

items: ELI5. A custom environment is your own practice world with your own rules. Wrappers change an existing one, such as scaling rewards, without rewriting it.
Here is a tiny custom environment. The agent stands on a line of cells and must walk to the right end. It is small enough to read in one go, and it follows every rule SB3 expects.
Check it before you train. check_env builds the checks SB3 relies on, such as whether reset and step return the right types and whether observations fit the declared space.
Register the class to build it by name, or just create it directly. For a time limit use TimeLimit or register with max_episode_steps.

from stable_baselines3.common.env_checker import check_env
env = LineWorld()
check_env(env, warn=True)          # silent means it passed

# Register to use gym.make("LineWorld-v0")
gym.register(id="LineWorld-v0", entry_point=LineWorld, max_episode_steps=50)
env = gym.make("LineWorld-v0")

items: Wrappers follow a simple pattern: subclass a wrapper type, override one method. Use gym.ObservationWrapper to change what the agent sees, gym.RewardWrapper to change the reward, and gym.ActionWrapper to change actions. Because they stack, you can add them one at a time and keep each easy to test.

Common bugs: observation dtype float64 when the space says float32, a reset that forgets to return info, a step that returns four values, and a Box with bounds the data goes outside. check_env finds most of these.

chapters.title: Deep RL and DQN
summary: When there are too many states for a table, a neural network approximates Q. It takes the observation and outputs one Q-value per action. Training is gradient descent on the TD error.

Naive training is unstable because consecutive samples are correlated and the target moves as the network changes. DQN fixes this with a replay buffer, which stores past experience and trains on random mini-batches, and a target network, a slowly updated copy used to compute targets.
DQN works for discrete actions only. It is exploring with epsilon-greedy, and it is the base for many improvements such as Double DQN and dueling networks.

glossary.def: Using a parametric model, such as a neural network, instead of a table to represent values or policies.
Deep Q-Network: Q-learning with a neural network, a replay buffer and a target network.
A memory of past transitions from which random mini-batches are sampled for training.
A delayed copy of the Q network used to compute stable training targets.
A small random group of transitions used for one gradient step.
Able to learn from old data collected by older versions of the policy, which is why a replay buffer works.
Slowly blending the online weights into the target network: target = tau * online + (1 - tau) * target.

keyPoints: Network input is the observation. Output is a Q-value for each action.
Loss is the squared (or Huber) difference between Q(s, a) and the target r + gamma * max Q_target(s').
Replay: store (s, a, r, s', done) and train on random samples.
Target network: update it every so many steps, or blend with a small tau.
DQN needs discrete actions. Use SAC, TD3 or PPO for continuous ones.
Start training after the buffer has some data (learning_starts in SB3).

items: ELI5. When there are too many states for a table, a neural network estimates the values instead. DQN adds a memory of past experience and a steady target so learning does not wobble.

A table fails when the observation is an image or a vector of real numbers. Instead of one row per state, a network learns a smooth function. Similar states get similar values, so what is learned in one place transfers to others. That is also what causes trouble: updating one state moves the values of many.

Two tricks make it work. First, the replay buffer. Experiences arrive in order and neighboring steps look alike, which makes gradient steps biased. Storing them and sampling at random mixes old and new, and lets each experience be reused many times.

Second, the target network. Look at the target: r + gamma times the maximum of Q at the next state. If the same network produces both the prediction and the target, every update moves the goalpost. So the target is computed by a frozen copy that is refreshed only now and then.

lesson.code:
# DQN training step in outline (PyTorch style)
s, a, r, s2, done = buffer.sample(batch_size)
with torch.no_grad():
    next_q = target_net(s2).max(dim=1).values
    target = r + gamma * (1 - done) * next_q
q = q_net(s).gather(1, a.unsqueeze(1)).squeeze(1)
loss = torch.nn.functional.smooth_l1_loss(q, target)
optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
if step % target_update_interval == 0:
    target_net.load_state_dict(q_net.state_dict())

items: Hyperparameters to know: the learning rate, the buffer size, the batch size, how often to update the target, how long epsilon decays, and learning_starts. In Stable-Baselines3 they are all constructor arguments of DQN.

Limits: DQN overestimates values (Double DQN reduces this), it is sample hungry, and it only handles a discrete action set. For robots with continuous controls you need a different family, which chapter 9 introduces.

summary: Stable-Baselines3, or SB3, is a library of reliable, well-tested RL algorithms built on PyTorch. It works directly with Gymnasium environments, so training is a few lines.
The core pattern: create an algorithm with a policy name and an environment, call learn with a number of timesteps, then use predict to act, evaluate_policy to measure, and save to keep the model.
Install with pip install stable-baselines3, or the extras bundle for plotting and logging. Recent releases need Python 3.10 or newer and a current PyTorch.

glossary.def: A PyTorch library of RL algorithms such as PPO, A2C, DQN, SAC, TD3 and DDPG.
The default network for vector observations: a multilayer perceptron.
Method that trains the model for total_timesteps environment steps.
Returns an action for an observation. Use deterministic=True when evaluating.
Helper that runs episodes and returns the mean and standard deviation of the episode reward.
Number of environment steps used for training, not the number of episodes.
SB3 wraps each environment so it can run in batches. Resets happen automatically.

keyPoints: pip install stable-baselines3 (add [extra] for plotting and TensorBoard support).
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, verbose=1); model.learn(total_timesteps=...).
model.predict(obs, deterministic=True) returns (action, state). Ignore the second value for feed-forward policies.
evaluate_policy(model, env, n_eval_episodes=10) returns (mean_reward, std_reward).
model.save("name") and PPO.load("name") keep and restore a model.
Evaluate on a separate environment instance from the one you trained on.

items: ELI5. Stable-Baselines3 is a library of ready-made agents. You pick one, give it an environment, and call learn. A quick way to get a baseline.
This is the hello world of SB3. It trains PPO on CartPole and watches the result. It usually reaches the maximum of 500 within about fifty thousand steps.

lesson.code: pip install "stable-baselines3[extra]"

import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.evaluation import evaluate_policy

env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, verbose=1, seed=0)
model.learn(total_timesteps=50_000)

eval_env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
mean_r, std_r = evaluate_policy(model, eval_env, n_eval_episodes=10, deterministic=True)
print(f"mean reward {mean_r:.1f} +/- {std_r:.1f}")

model.save("ppo_cartpole")
del model
model = PPO.load("ppo_cartpole")

items: Using the model yourself. predict takes one observation and returns an action. The second value is a recurrent state which is None for normal policies.

lesson.code:
env = gym.make("CartPole-v1", render_mode="human")
obs, info = env.reset()
done = False
while not done:
    action, _ = model.predict(obs, deterministic=True)
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(action)
    done = terminated or truncated
env.close()

items: Behind the scenes SB3 wraps your environment in a vectorized environment and a Monitor, which records episode reward and length. The vectorized API differs slightly from Gymnasium: reset returns only observations, step returns four values and resets finished environments by itself. You see this if you call model.get_env().

Switching algorithm is a one-word change. DQN for CartPole, SAC for Pendulum. The policy string stays MlpPolicy for vector inputs, CnnPolicy for images, and MultiInputPolicy for dictionary observations. Use policy_kwargs to change the network, for example policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=[64, 64]).

lesson.code:
from stable_baselines3 import DQN, SAC
dqn = DQN("MlpPolicy", "CartPole-v1", verbose=0)       # a string id works as well
sac = SAC("MlpPolicy", "Pendulum-v1", verbose=0)
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", "CartPole-v1",
            policy_kwargs=dict(net_arch=[64, 64]), learning_rate=3e-4)

items: Treat total_timesteps as a budget and judge the model by evaluation, not by the training log alone. Always check how the reward curve changes with different seeds. RL results vary a lot from run to run.

chapters.title: Policy gradients, PPO and choosing an algorithm

maps.title: Algorithm families
links: PPO | limits | Policy change per update
Off-policy | reuses data | Often via replay buffer [ch7]

summary: Value-based methods such as DQN learn Q and act greedily. Policy-gradient methods learn the policy directly: they nudge the probability of actions up when they led to a high return and down when they led to a low one.

Actor-critic methods add a critic, a value function that tells how much better an action was than expected. That difference is called the advantage and it reduces noise. A2C and PPO are actor-critic methods.

PPO, proximal policy optimization, clips the update so the new policy stays close to the old one. It is simple, stable, works for discrete and continuous actions, and is a strong default. For continuous control SAC and TD3 are often more sample efficient.

glossary.def: A method that adjusts policy parameters in the direction that increases expected return.
The part of the agent that chooses actions, the policy network.
The part that estimates values, used to judge the actor's actions.
How much better an action was than the average action in that state: Q minus V.
Proximal Policy Optimization. Policy gradient with a clipped objective that keeps updates small.
Learns only from data gathered by the current policy, so old data is thrown away.
A reward for keeping the policy random enough, to encourage exploration.
Soft Actor-Critic: an off-policy actor-critic for continuous actions that maximizes reward plus entropy.

keyPoints: PPO and A2C are on-policy. DQN, SAC, TD3 and DDPG are off-policy.
DQN: discrete actions only. SAC, TD3, DDPG: continuous only. PPO and A2C: both.
PPO clip objective: min(ratio * A, clip(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * A). Typical eps is 0.2.
Start with PPO. Try SAC for continuous control when samples are expensive.
On-policy methods usually want many parallel environments.
Advantage estimates (GAE) trade bias against variance with lambda, typically 0.95.

items: ELI5. Policy gradient methods learn the behaviour directly instead of values. PPO is a popular steady choice. Pick an algorithm by the action type and how much data you can afford.

A policy-gradient agent uses a network that outputs action probabilities. After running some episodes you increase the probability of each action in proportion to how good the outcome was. The idea is called REINFORCE. It is simple and noisy, because a single lucky episode can push the policy the wrong way.

To cut the noise, subtract a baseline. If the average outcome in a state is 10 and this action gave 12, the advantage is plus 2, and the action becomes more likely. If it gave 8, it becomes less likely. The critic network learns that baseline V(s). Together the actor and the critic form an actor-critic.

The danger with policy gradients is a step too big. One bad update can wreck the policy, and since the new data comes from the new policy, it may never recover. PPO guards against this. It computes the ratio of the new probability to the old one for each action and clips it to the range 1 minus epsilon to 1 plus epsilon, so there is no gain from moving further than that.

lesson.code:
# PPO clipped objective for one sample (maximize this)
ratio = new_prob / old_prob
clipped = max(1 - eps, min(ratio, 1 + eps))
objective = min(ratio * advantage, clipped * advantage)

items: Each PPO iteration collects n_steps from each environment, then runs several epochs of mini-batch updates on that data, then throws it away. That is on-policy learning. The defaults in SB3 are n_steps 2048, batch_size 64, n_epochs 10, gamma 0.99, gae_lambda 0.95 and clip_range 0.2, which work well for many problems.
How to choose?

lesson.code:
Algorithm | Actions            | Data      | Notes
PPO       | discrete, continuous | on-policy | strong default, parallel envs
A2C       | discrete, continuous | on-policy | simple, fast, noisier
DQN       | discrete             | off-policy| image games, replay buffer
SAC       | continuous           | off-policy| sample efficient, robust
TD3       | continuous           | off-policy| deterministic, careful tuning
DDPG      | continuous           | off-policy| older, sensitive

items: SB3 gives all of these under the same interface. Extra algorithms live in the sb3-contrib package, for example recurrent PPO, TRPO and QR-DQN.

maps.title: A real training setup

summary: Real projects train many environments in parallel with make_vec_env, evaluate on a separate environment, save the best model and log curves to TensorBoard. SB3's callbacks do the periodic work without you rewriting the training loop.
Always use a Monitor so episode reward and length are recorded, a separate evaluation environment so you test what you train, and several random seeds because RL results vary widely between runs.
VecNormalize normalizes observations and rewards, which helps in many continuous control tasks. If you use it, save and load its statistics together with the model.

glossary.def: Helper that builds several copies of an environment, each wrapped with a Monitor.
Runs several environments one after another in a single process.
Runs each environment in its own process for real parallelism.
An object whose methods are called during training, for example to evaluate or save.
Evaluates the model every eval_freq steps and can save the best model.
A web dashboard for training curves. Enable it with tensorboard_log.
A wrapper that keeps running statistics to normalize observations and rewards.
A number that fixes random choices so a run can be repeated.

keyPoints: Use make_vec_env("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8) to collect data faster.
Evaluate on a separate environment, not the training one.
EvalCallback(eval_env, best_model_save_path=..., eval_freq=...) keeps the best model.
Log with tensorboard_log="./tb" and view with tensorboard --logdir ./tb.
Run at least 3 to 5 seeds before believing a result.
When using VecNormalize, save it: env.save("vecnormalize.pkl") and load it for evaluation with training=False.

items: ELI5. Training in practice means running many copies of the world at once, saving checkpoints and watching curves. Callbacks let you act during training.
Here is a complete small training script with the features you will want in any project. Read it top to bottom.

lesson.code:
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.env_util import make_vec_env
from stable_baselines3.common.callbacks import EvalCallback, CheckpointCallback, StopTrainingOnRewardThreshold
from stable_baselines3.common.evaluation import evaluate_policy
from stable_baselines3.common.monitor import Monitor
import gymnasium as gym

if __name__ == "__main__":                       # needed for SubprocVecEnv on Windows and macOS
    train_env = make_vec_env("CartPole-v1", n_envs=8, seed=0)
    eval_env = Monitor(gym.make("CartPole-v1"))

    stop = StopTrainingOnRewardThreshold(reward_threshold=475, verbose=1)
    evalcb = EvalCallback(eval_env, callback_on_new_best=stop,
                          best_model_save_path="./best/", log_path="./logs/",
                          eval_freq=5_000, n_eval_episodes=10, deterministic=True)
    ckpt = CheckpointCallback(save_freq=20_000, save_path="./ckpt/", name_prefix="ppo_cp")

    model = PPO("MlpPolicy", train_env, tensorboard_log="./tb/", seed=0, verbose=1)
    model.learn(total_timesteps=200_000, callback=[evalcb, ckpt])

    best = PPO.load("./best/best_model")
    print(evaluate_policy(best, eval_env, n_eval_episodes=20))

items: Note about eval_freq. With 8 parallel environments, eval_freq counts calls of the callback, which happen once per step of every environment together. To evaluate every N total timesteps divide by the number of environments: eval_freq = max(N // n_envs, 1).
To watch training run tensorboard in a second terminal.

lesson.code:
pip install tensorboard
tensorboard --logdir ./tb/
# then open http://localhost:6006

items: Things to watch on the curves: ep_rew_mean should rise. For PPO, approx_kl and clip_fraction show how big updates are, explained_variance shows how well the critic predicts returns, and entropy_loss shows whether the policy has become too deterministic too early. A flat or falling ep_rew_mean over a long time is a sign to check rewards, learning rate and seeds.

Normalization. Reward scales and observation ranges vary wildly between tasks. VecNormalize keeps running averages and rescales. Remember that the statistics are part of the model: evaluating without them gives bad results.

lesson.code:
from stable_baselines3.common.vec_env import DummyVecEnv, VecNormalize

venv = VecNormalize(DummyVecEnv([lambda: gym.make("Pendulum-v1")]), norm_obs=True, norm_reward=True)
model = SAC("MlpPolicy", venv).learn(50_000)
model.save("sac_pendulum"); venv.save("vecnormalize.pkl")

# later, for evaluation
venv = VecNormalize.load("vecnormalize.pkl", DummyVecEnv([lambda: gym.make("Pendulum-v1")]))
venv.training = False; venv.norm_reward = False

items: Reproducibility. Pass seed to the algorithm and to make_vec_env, and expect small differences anyway on GPU. For reporting, run several seeds and show the mean with its spread. Compare algorithms with the same budget of timesteps.

chapters.title: Reward design, debugging and pitfalls

maps.title: Why training fails
links: Reward design | decides | What the agent learns
Bug in env | looks like | Bad algorithm

summary: An agent optimizes exactly the reward you wrote, not the one you meant. A badly designed reward gets exploited: the agent finds a loophole that scores high without doing the task. This is called reward hacking or specification gaming.

Sparse rewards, where feedback comes only at the very end, make learning slow. Reward shaping adds intermediate signals, but it must reward progress toward the real goal and not creative shortcuts. Potential-based shaping is the safe form.

When training fails, suspect the environment and the reward first, then the observation scaling, then the hyperparameters, and only then the algorithm. A short checklist and small test environments save time.

glossary.def: Adding extra reward signals that guide the agent toward the goal.
A reward that is zero almost everywhere and nonzero only on success.
When the agent exploits a loophole in the reward to score high without solving the task.
Shaping of the form gamma * phi(s') - phi(s). It does not change the best policy.
Starting with easy versions of a task and making it harder as the agent improves.
Performing well only on the starting states or random numbers seen in training.
A setting chosen by you, not learned, such as the learning rate or n_steps.

keyPoints: Write the reward for the outcome you want, then ask how it could be gamed.
Dense hints help, but mistakes in shaping teach the wrong behavior.
Log and watch the agent. Plot an episode, render a video, read the numbers.
Test the environment by hand before training: step with fixed actions and check rewards.
Solve a smaller version of the task first.
Change one thing at a time and keep the seed fixed when comparing.

items: ELI5. The agent does what the reward says, not what you meant. Careful reward design and debugging prevent silly shortcuts. Always watch the agent play.

The classic story is a boat racing game where the agent learned to spin in circles collecting small bonus items, scoring higher than any agent that finished the race. The reward said points, not finish. The agent did what the reward said.

A simpler example: a cleaning robot rewarded for dust collected could learn to dump dust and re-collect it. A walking robot rewarded for forward speed might learn to fall forward as fast as it can. These are not bugs in the learning algorithm. They are bugs in the reward.

Sparse rewards are the opposite problem. In a maze with a reward only at the exit, a random agent might never find it, and nothing is learned. Shaping adds hints, such as a small reward for getting closer to the goal. Do it carefully. If you reward distance reduction and also forget a penalty for loops, the agent can step back and forth forever collecting points.

The safe version is potential-based shaping. Define a potential phi(s), for example minus the distance to the goal. Add gamma times phi of the next state minus phi of the current state to the reward. Stepping away costs exactly what stepping back gains, so loops give nothing, and the best policy is unchanged.

lesson.code:
# Potential-based shaping inside step()
def phi(pos):             # potential: higher is closer to the goal
    return -abs(self.goal - pos)

shaped = reward + self.gamma * phi(new_pos) - phi(old_pos)

items: A debugging checklist. First, run check_env and fix every warning. Second, step the environment by hand with a fixed action list and read the rewards and flags.
Third, confirm that a trivial policy, such as always going right in LineWorld, gets the reward you expect.
Fourth, look at observation scale: values near zero to one or minus one to one train faster than values in the thousands.
Fifth, try a known-good algorithm on a known-good environment to check your install. Sixth, only then tune the learning rate, the n_steps or the network size.

Other pitfalls. Reporting one lucky seed. Evaluating with exploration noise on. Mixing up terminated and truncated in a custom environment. Training for too few steps: CartPole takes thousands, Atari takes millions. Using a policy trained with VecNormalize without the saved statistics. A reward whose scale is so large that gradients explode.
Finally, remember the safety side: an agent in the real world will exploit unexpected loopholes in the real world. Test in simulation, add limits and keep a human in the loop.

summary: You now know the loop, the math, tabular and deep value learning, policy gradients, the SB3 toolkit and how to build and debug environments. The best next step is to build something of your own.

Useful extensions: continuous control tasks with SAC, image-based tasks with CnnPolicy, the RL Zoo for tuned hyperparameters and training scripts, sb3-contrib for extra algorithms, and multi-agent and offline RL when your problem calls for it.

items: ELI5. Where next: harder environments, safer methods and real robots. Each step builds on the loop you now know.

Suggested projects, in rising difficulty: a grid or line world of your own with Q-learning; a custom environment trained with PPO; Pendulum or MountainCarContinuous with SAC; LunarLander with PPO or DQN; an Atari game with CnnPolicy; a robotics simulation. At each step write down what you expect before running.

items: Atari needs extra packages (the ale-py package and the ROM license acceptance that comes with it) and a lot of training steps, often millions, so a GPU helps. Check the current installation notes before starting.
For continuous control the RL Zoo contains tuned settings such as network size, learning rate and noise choices for many tasks. Start with those rather than guessing.

How to keep learning. Keep a notebook of experiments: environment version, algorithm, hyperparameters, seed and result. Reproduce a published result before inventing your own. When you hit something odd, shrink the problem until you can explain it.
Thank you for learning with Lilith. Use the final exam to check yourself, and revisit the chapters where your score was lowest.

sandbox.title: Algorithm cheat sheet
sandbox.intro: A scripted lookup tool, not a real Python shell. Try: algo ppo, compare, defaults ppo, spaces

out: algo <ppo|a2c|dqn|sac|td3|ddpg>   what it is and when to use it
compare                          table of action spaces and data use
defaults ppo                     main PPO defaults in SB3
PPO: on-policy actor-critic with a clipped objective.
Actions: discrete or continuous. Use as a strong default.
A2C: on-policy actor-critic, synchronous advantage updates.
Actions: discrete or continuous. Simple and fast, often noisier than PPO.
DQN: off-policy value-based with replay buffer and target network.
Actions: discrete only. Good for games and image inputs.
SAC: off-policy actor-critic with an entropy bonus.
Actions: continuous only. Sample efficient and robust for control.
TD3: off-policy deterministic actor-critic with twin critics.
DDPG: off-policy deterministic actor-critic, an ancestor of TD3.
Actions: continuous only. Sensitive to settings.
Unknown algorithm. Try: ppo a2c dqn sac td3 ddpg
(check your SB3 version's docs to confirm)
